coredata.dc:description: Bisphenol-A (BPA) was first synthesized in the 1890s and has been used in many plastic products. However, BPA is known to act as an endocrine disruptor and has been found to be toxic to human health. Many alternative substances have been developed to replace BPA, but it is still widely used worldwide. In this study, we identified the potential cytotoxicity of BPA by evaluating toxicity using human keratinocytes. Also, we evaluated cytotoxicity of BPA substitutes to determine their suitability as an alternative to BPA. The proliferation assay using the 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide, flow cytometry and western blot analysis showed that BPA significantly affect cell viability, induction of apoptotic fraction and increased activation of DNA-damage marker protein. In addition, through the same experiments, the substitutes of BPA were shown to be significantly less toxic than BPA, and the least toxicity was observed with 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanol (CHDM) and terephthalic acid (TPA). In conclusion, this study suggests that cytotoxicity of BPA induces apoptosis of human keratinocytes, and that CHDM and TPA are the most suitable substitutes for BPA.

ce:caption.ce:simple-para: Effects of bisphenol A (BPA) and its substitutes on cell viability of human keratinocytes. HaCaT cells were seeded at a density of 2 × 103 cells/well in 96-well plates and left to settle. After 24 h, the cells were treated with various concentrations (2, 5, 10, 50, 100 μg/mL) of BPA or its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD and TPA) for 24 h. Cell viability was determined by MTT assay after 24 h of exposure (*P < 0.05).

Effects of BPA and its substitutes on colony-forming abilities. HaCaT cells were seeded at a density of 200 cells/well in 6-well plates and treated with 20 μg/mL of BPA or its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD and TPA). After 10 days, the cells were washed and stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 30 min (*P < 0.05).

Quantification of apoptotic fractions after treatment with BPA and its substitutes in HaCaT. (A / B) HaCaT cells were seeded at a density of 8 × 105 cells in 100 mm dishes, and BPA and its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD, and TPA) were added at 50 μg/mL for 24 h. After 24 h, the cells were harvested, washed with PBS, fixed in methanol, and incubated in PBS containing 40 μg/mL propidium iodide and 100 μg/mL RNase A. Propidium iodide-labeled nuclei were analyzed by flow cytometry (*P < 0.05). (B) The apoptotic fraction with each chemical was quantified (*P < 0.05).

DNA damage and activation of pro-apoptotic proteins with BPA. HaCaT cells were seeded at a density of 4 × 105 cells in 60 mm dishes and incubated for 24 h. Cells were treated with BPA or its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD, and TPA) at a concentration of 50 or 100 μg/mL for 24 h. After 24 h of treatment, levels of PARP and caspase-3–cleaved proteins were measured by western blotting. Actin was used as a loading control.

ce:section.ce:para: Bisphenol-A (BPA) was first synthesized as a synthetic estrogen in the 1890s and is currently used as a polymerization agent for polycarbonate or epoxy resin. In the modern world, BPA is used in a wide variety of applications from thermal paper to food packaging (Rochester, 2013; Vandenberg et al., 2012). However, BPA has been known to act as an endocrine disruptor by mimicking estrogen, as it was originally synthesized as a synthetic estrogen (Vinas et al., 2012). Further studies have shown that BPA binds not only to estrogen receptors, but also to androgen receptors and thyroid receptors. Despite the continued research on the effects of BPA on human health, BPA is still one of the most produced chemical compounds in the world, with 2.2 million tonnes produced in 2002 and 5.5 million tonnes estimated to have been produced in 2011 (Rochester, 2013; Rubin, 2011).

Accordingly, various substances have been proposed to replace BPA (Ng et al., 2015). We selected five candidates to compare to BPA in cytotoxicity experiments. The selected candidates were 1,4-cyclohexanedimethanol (CHDM), D-isosorbide, dimethyl terephthalate (DMTP), 2,2,4,4-tetramethyl-1,3-cyclobutanediol (TMCD), and terephthalic acid (TPA). CHDM, TMCD, and DMTP are the monomers used to synthesize Eastman's Tritan™ copolyester. Tritan™ was the first polymer synthesized to replace polycarbonate using BPA. TPA, which is the first metabolite of DMTP, can also be used for polyester synthesis (Osimitz et al., 2012). A previous study showed that DMTP, CHDM, and TMCD had no androgenic or estrogenic effects on humans (Ng et al., 2015; Osimitz et al., 2015). D-isosorbide has also been used in place of BPA for synthesizing polycarbonates (Nelson and Long, 2012).

Although the toxicity of BPA as an endocrine disruptor has been widely studied, few studies have compared BPA with its substitutes in terms of skin toxicity. Among human tissues, skin is most likely to be exposed to the external environment. In this study, we investigated the cytotoxicity of BPA and its substitutes using HaCaT, a keratinocyte cell line derived from human skin. We examined whether BPA affects cell growth by assessing cell viability with MTT assays. In addition, we tested whether BPA induces apoptosis by flow cytometry of PI-labeled nuclei and by western blot analysis of changes in activation of apoptotic proteins, poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) and caspase-3. PARP and caspase-3 are well-known apoptosis marker for in vitro studies (Boulares et al., 1999). Using this approach, we confirmed the cytotoxicity of BPA and compared its cytotoxicity with that of its substitutes in order to suggest appropriate alternatives for BPA.

HaCaT human keratinocytes were kindly provided from Professor JM Choi (Hanyang University, Seoul, Korea). Cells were maintained in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle's Medium (Corning, Corning, NY, USA) containing 10% fetal bovine serum (Youngin Frontier, Seoul, Korea), 100 U/mL penicillin (Corning), and 100 mg/mL streptomycin (Corning). All cell lines were incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO2 in a humidified atmosphere.

Antibodies against p-Histone H2A.X (Ser139), PARP, and caspase-3 were purchased from Cell Signaling Technology (Beverly, MA, USA). Antibodies against actin and β-tubulin were purchased from Santa Cruz Biotechnology (Santa Cruz, CA, USA). HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies against mouse IgG, rabbit IgG were purchased form Cell Signaling Technology (Beverly, MA, USA). BPA and its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD, TPA) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA). Purity of all chemicals is more than 99%. For treating the cells, BPA was dissolved in ethanol; CHDM, D-isosorbide, and TMCD were dissolved in distilled water; TPA was dissolved in DMSO; and DMTP was dissolved in DMSO + Tween 20 (29:1). All chemicals were used at concentrations of 10 mg/mL and 100 mg/mL. For control groups, an equal volume of each vehicle was used.

Cell proliferation was measured using 3-(4,5-dimethylthiazol-2-yl)-2,5-diphenyltetrazolium bromide (MTT) thiazolyl blue assays. Cells were seeded in 96-well culture plates at 2 × 103 cells per well and treated with various concentrations (2, 5, 10, 50, 100 μg/mL) of BPA or its substitutes (CHDM, D-isosorbide, DMTP, TMCD and TPA) for 24 h. After treatment with BPA or its substitutes, 10 mg/mL MTT (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to 100 μL of culture medium for 3 h incubation at 37 °C. After removing the medium, dimethyl sulfoxide (Sigma-Aldrich) was added to dissolve the formazan, and the optical density was measured at 590 nm using a Multiskan EX (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). Experimental concentrations of each chemicals were used in 1/1000 vol of the total culture media and control vehicle was used in the same amount. Experiments were repeated three times.

Cells were seeded at 200 cells per well in 6-well culture plates and incubated with BPA or its substitutes for 10 days at 37 °C in a CO2 incubator. After 10 days, the cells were washed with PBS and stained with 0.5% crystal violet for 30 min. The cells were then washed twice with PBS and observed with an optical microscope. The experiments were performed in triplicate and quantitated by counting the number of colonies.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Cell cycle analysis by flow cytometry
ce:section.ce:para: Cells were harvested, washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), fixed in 100% methanol overnight at −20 °C, and incubated in PBS containing 40 μg/mL propidium iodide (PI) and 100 μg/mL RNase for 10 min at room temperature (RT). Cell cycle analyses were performed on a BD FACSCanto II (BD Biosciences, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA), and the data were analyzed using FlowJo software (FlowJo LLC, Ashland, OR, USA). Experiments were repeated three times.

Cells were washed once with PBS and lysed with lysis buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 0.1 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl, 1% NP-40, 0.1% Triton X-100, 0.1% SDS, 20 mM NaF, 1 mM Na3VO4, 1× protease inhibitor; Roche, Basel, Switzerland). Equal amounts of protein in cell lysates were determined by standardization with the BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Proteins were resolved by SDS-PAGE and transferred to nitrocellulose membranes (Whatman GmbH, Dassel, Germany). After blocking with 5% skim milk in TBST at RT for 1 h, membranes were incubated with primary antibodies (Diluted to 1: 1000 in 5% BSA) overnight at 4 °C, followed by 2 h incubation with HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (Diluted to 1: 2000 in 5% skim milk) at RT. Protein bands were visualized with Dyne ECL (Dyne, Seongnam, Korea).

All experiments were performed in triplicate. Data from MTT assays, colony formation assays, and cell cycle analyses are expressed as means ± standard deviations. Comparison of results from experimental groups versus control groups was done using student's t-test. A value of p < 0.05 was marked as a significant difference in each figure.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of BPA and its substitutes on viability of human keratinocytes
ce:section.ce:para: To measure the cytotoxicity of BPA and its substitutes, we first treated HaCaT cells with these chemicals at 2, 5, 10, 50 and 100 μg/mL for 24 h and then analyzed cell viability using MTT assays ( Fig. 1). Each of the chemicals was diluted in various vehicles, and it was confirmed that each vehicle did not affect cell viability at a concentration level of 0.5% −1% (v/v) (Data not shown). The results show that low doses of all six chemicals did not significantly affect cell viability. However, as the concentration of BPA increased, cell viability of HaCaT cells was significantly decreased. Cell viability of HaCaT cells was 60% and 12% after exposure to 50 μg/mL and 100 μg/mL BPA, respectively. High doses of D-isosorbide, DMPT, and TMCD also influenced cell viability of HaCaT cells. Cell viability of HaCaT cells was 80% after exposure to 100 μg/mL D-isosorbide; 80% after exposure to 100 μg/mL DMPT; 77%, 75% and 68% after exposure to 10, 50 and 100 μg/mL TMCD, respectively. However, with those treatments, cell viability decreased by only approximately 30%, even at the highest dose used for all treatments (100 μg/mL). With BPA, the cell viability decreased by more than 80% at 100 μg/mL. CHDM and TPA did not affect cell viability at 100 μg/mL.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Effects of BPA and its substitute on colony-forming ability
ce:section.ce:para: Next, we performed colony-forming assays with all 6 chemicals. All materials were used at a concentration of 20 μg/mL, and the results were similar to those obtained from the MTT assays ( Fig. 2and Fig. S1). The BPA-treated well had nearly zero colonies after 10 days of incubation. In addition, the wells treated with D-isosorbide, DMTP, and TMCD showed a decrease in colony number compared to the control treatments. CHDM and TPA had no negative effect on colony number. These results indicate that BPA affects cell viability and growth and has a stronger effect than its substitutes, especially CHDM and TPA.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Quantification of apoptotic cells after treatment with BPA and its substitutes
ce:section.ce:para: Next, we performed a flow cytometry analysis to determine whether BPA and its substitutes affect apoptotic processes ( Fig. 3A,B). Before flow cytometry analysis, HaCaT cells were treated with BPA and its substitutes at 50 μg/mL for 24 h. BPA-treated cells exhibited a significantly increased apoptotic fraction compared to control cells, and all other cells states decreased compared with control. DMTP- and TMCD-treated cells showed slightly increased apoptotic fractions. There were no significant differences in apoptotic fraction between control and D-isosorbide-, CHDM-, or TPA-treated cells.

ce:section.ce:section-title: BPA, DNA damage, and activation of pro-apoptotic proteins
ce:section.ce:para: To further investigate molecular evidence for apoptosis and DNA damage after the chemical treatments, we used western blot analysis to assess cleavage of caspase-3 and the DNA-damage marker PARP ( Fig. 4). The results showed that cleaved PARP and caspase-3 were increased dose-dependently in BPA-, D-isosorbide-, TMCD-, and DMTP-treated cells. In the case of TMCD, cleavage of caspase-3 level was difficult to be distinguished between 50 μg/mL and 100 μg/mL treated samples. However, quantification of western blot band with ImageJ showed that at concentrations of 50 μg/mL and 100 μg/mL, cleaved form of caspase-3 increased in 4.5, and 5.8 times, respectively, compared to control. Levels of cleaved caspase-3 and PARP were higher in BPA- and TMCD-treated cells. CHDM and TPA did not affect apoptosis or DNA damage at the molecular level. All these results suggest that high concentrations of BPA have a significant effect on cell growth and apoptosis, and its substitutes also affect cell growth and apoptosis but with less effect than BPA. Furthermore, CHDM and TPA have almost no negative effects on cell growth and apoptosis even at a concentration of 100 μg/mL.

BPA is mainly used in the production of polycarbonate and epoxy resins. Thus, it is components of various products used in modern world, for example, polycarbonate bottle, food container, toys and thermal paper (Hoekstra and Simoneau, 2013; Michalowicz, 2014). BPA in household plastic products can contact the human skin, even under normal conditions, due to incomplete polymerization or manufacturing process problems as well as degradation via exposure to heat or acidic conditions (Vandenberg et al., 2010; Welshons et al., 2006). The effects of BPA as an endocrine disruptor have been well studied to date (Bonefeld-Jorgensen et al., 2007; Richter et al., 2007). BPA binds competitively to the nuclear estrogen receptor (ER) with 17-beta-estradiol (E2) (Michalowicz, 2014). Early studies have shown that BPA has a lower affinity for ER than E2 (Andersen et al., 1999; Kuiper et al., 1998), but recent studies have shown that it disrupts various cellular responses even at low concentrations (Alonso-Magdalena et al., 2012). Therefore, many substitutes have been created and commercialized (Ng et al., 2015; Osimitz et al., 2012). However, BPA is still being produced around the world, and there are still many BPA-containing products that humans contact daily (Huang et al., 2012). In addition, there is not much toxicity assessment of the substitutes of BPA, so it is not enough to evaluate the suitability as an alternative to replace BPA. Under these circumstances, we assessed the cytotoxicity of BPA and its substitutes to establish biochemical and cell biological standards for measuring the toxicity of BPA and its substitutes.

The cells we used for the experiments were HaCaT cells, which are derived from human skin and can be used to indirectly assess the effects of BPA on the skin (Boukamp et al., 1988; Schoop et al., 1999). In this experiment, we confirmed that BPA has a very significant effect on HaCaT growth and apoptosis at more than 20 μg/mL. Concentration of 20 μg/mL is very high concentration compare to the environmental condition. Because, the maximum tolerable concentration of BPA in the effluent of a waste-water treatment plant is approximately 400 μg/L (Corrales et al., 2015). Therefore, we can conclude that the risk of skin cytotoxicity with BPA is not significant at environmental concentrations. In the MTT assay, most substances did not have a significant effect on cell viability at concentrations below 20 μg/mL. However, the colony-formation assay showed a significant decrease in HaCaT cells upon treatment with BPA and other substitutes at a concentration of 20 μg/mL. Colony-formation assays generally measure longer-term cytotoxicity than MTT assays. Therefore, we may be assured that there is a problem when the skin cells are chronically exposed to BPA or other substitutes. Therefore, based on these experimental results, it is difficult to conclude that BPA is generally safe for human skin.

We used five different BPA substitutes in this study. CHDM, TMCD, DMTP, TPA and D-isosorbide. CHDM, DMTP and TMCD are well known as major raw materials for polyester plastic produced by Eastman chemical in US (Osimitz et al., 2012). CHDM, a chemical made by reduction of DMTP is used as a monomer to synthesize polyethylene terephthalate (PET) which can make plastic bottles (Turner, 2004). Compared to BPA, TMCD is thermally and mechanically stable and is also used as a monomer to make polyester (Hoppens et al., 2004). TPA is also known to be used in the production of PET and is thermostable (Sheehan, 2012). D-isosorbide has high thermal stability and can be used to produce epoxy resin instead of BPA (Rose and Palkovits, 2012). Since all five substitutes are known to have high thermal stability compared to BPA, they are less released to the monomer by heat than BPA. Therefore, even if BPA and its substitutes show the same toxicity, substitutes will be used more safely because they are less degraded by heat in actual environment.

The results of the cytotoxicity evaluation of BPA substitutes indicated that a significant level of cytotoxicity was also observed at the highest concentration tested (100 μg/mL), but the degree of toxicity was significantly lower than that of BPA. In fact, TPA and CHDM did not show any toxicity at that concentration. In the cell viability assay using MTT, the toxicities associated with most of the substitutes were not observed at 50 μg/mL but increased apoptotic protein activities were observed in TMCD-treated cells. This suggests that alternative agents may also show cytotoxicity when used at similar concentrations to BPA and may show higher cytotoxicity at prolonged exposure. However, considering the difference from BPA, we conclude that the substitutes used in this study generally have lower cytotoxicities than BPA.

The substitutes used in this experiment are already commercially available (Osimitz et al., 2012). Among them, D-isosorbide, TMCD, and DMTP showed some cytotoxicity. Therefore, TPA and CHDM might instead be appropriate for BPA substitutes. However, more specific toxicity evaluations including in vivo experiments or long-term experiments should be performed before replacements can be chosen for BPA at a commercial scale.
